questions.q: In function f(amount: number | string) { if (typeof amount === "string") return; … }, what is the type of amount on the lines after the if?
questions.explain: A variable keeps its declared type, but at each point TypeScript tracks what it can still be. The if returns for strings, so only number reaches the following lines.
options: Still number | string: the declared type never changes
number: the declared type is unchanged, but the narrowed type at that point is number
string, because that was the last type checked

questions.q: Why does if (typeof tags === "object") return tags.length; fail to compile when tags is string | string[] | null?
questions.explain: JavaScript reports "object" for null. TypeScript models that, so null survives the check and you get 'tags' is possibly 'null'. Check tags !== null too, or use Array.isArray.
options: Because arrays are not objects in JavaScript
Because typeof null is "object", so inside the branch tags is string[] | null
Because typeof cannot narrow unions with more than two members
Because length does not exist on arrays in strict mode

questions.q: Which of these is not a value the JavaScript typeof operator can return?
questions.explain: typeof returns one of eight strings: string, number, bigint, boolean, symbol, undefined, object and function. Arrays are "object"; use Array.isArray to recognise them.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: null and the array both pass typeof value === "object", and the inner check separates them. 0 is a number and "" a string; typeof does not care whether a value is falsy.
options: list of 0 | list of 2 | amount 0 | text

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: 0 is falsy, so a real balance of ₦0 goes to the "not available" branch. The code compiles because TypeScript only promises that balance is a number inside the if. Use balance !== null instead.

questions.q: For quantity: number | undefined, what is the type of quantity in the else branch of if (quantity) { … } else { … }?
questions.explain: A falsy number (0 or NaN) also reaches the else branch, so TypeScript cannot remove number there. The type is still number | undefined, which is the compiler reminding you that "falsy" is not "missing".

questions.q: A daily transfer limit of 0 means "this account may not transfer". What does this print?
questions.explain: || replaces every falsy value, including 0, so the blocked account suddenly gets ₦50,000. ?? only replaces null and undefined.

questions.q: Which value is truthy, and so passes if (value)?
questions.explain: "0" is a non-empty string, so it is truthy. The falsy values are false, 0, -0, 0n, NaN, "", null and undefined. This is why if (amount) on a string amount lets "0" through.

questions.q: What does if (to == null) return; remove from the type of to: string | null | undefined on the following lines?
questions.explain: Loose equality with null is true for exactly null and undefined, and TypeScript narrows accordingly. It is the one common, safe use of ==.

questions.q: to is a string and fallback is string | number. Inside if (to === fallback) { … }, what is the type of fallback?
questions.explain: === can only be true when both sides are the same type, and to is a string. So equality narrows both sides to the types they have in common.

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: "iban" in account is true only for the foreign account. After that branch returns, only Local is left, so accountNumber and bankCode can be read without another check.

questions.q: Why can you not write value instanceof Account when Account is an interface?
questions.explain: instanceof checks a constructor's prototype at runtime, so it needs a class, which is a real JavaScript value. Interfaces and type aliases vanish when TypeScript compiles; check their properties instead.
options: Because instanceof only works on primitive values
Because interfaces are erased: there is no Account value at runtime for instanceof to use

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: An InsufficientFundsError is also an Error, so the first check catches it and the specific branch never runs. Put the most specific class first. A thrown string is not an Error at all.

questions.q: A Money class has amount and currency properties. What is JSON.parse('{"amount": 5, "currency": "NGN"}') instanceof Money?
questions.explain: instanceof looks at the prototype chain, not the shape. Data from JSON is never an instance of your classes; check its properties, or build an instance from it after validating.
options: true, because the object has every property of Money
false: JSON.parse creates plain objects, whose prototype is Object.prototype

questions.q: You model payments as card, transfer and wallet objects. Which design narrows most reliably and gives exhaustiveness checks?
questions.explain: A discriminant is explicit, works on plain data from JSON, survives refactoring, and lets the compiler prove a switch covers every member. in works, but guesses from shape.
options: Distinguish them by which optional properties are present, with in
Give each member a kind property with its own literal value, and switch on it
Make them classes and check with instanceof everywhere, including data from JSON
Use one type with every property optional and check each one

questions.q: A function with return type string ends with a switch (payment.kind) that returns in every case and has no default. Someone adds "ussd" to the union. What happens?
questions.explain: While every kind is covered, TypeScript knows the end of the function is unreachable. Once "ussd" is not covered, the end becomes reachable and string does not include undefined, so you get error TS2366.
options: Nothing: the function returns undefined for USSD at runtime and tsc is silent
tsc reports that the function lacks an ending return statement
tsc removes the function from the output

questions.q: Does const { kind } = payment; if (kind === "card") { payment.last4 } compile, when payment is a discriminated union parameter that is never reassigned?
questions.explain: TypeScript connects a destructured const discriminant to the object it came from, as long as neither can be reassigned. With let the link could break, so it does not narrow.
options: Yes: TypeScript narrows payment through a destructured const discriminant
No: narrowing only works on payment.kind written in full

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Each guard clause returns early, so the code below it only runs when the check failed. 1000 is not greater than 1000, so the withdrawal goes through and leaves 0.
options:
new balance 0
new balance 990
no account

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Assigning narrows a let variable to the type of what was assigned, within its declared type. After reference = 7 it is a number, so toFixed compiles.

questions.q: Does this compile? function f(v: string | number) { const isText = typeof v === "string"; return isText ? v.toUpperCase() : v.toFixed(2); }
questions.explain: TypeScript (since 4.4) follows aliased conditions, as long as the condition is a const and the narrowed value is a const or an unassigned parameter.
options: Yes: a condition stored in a const still narrows a parameter that is never reassigned
No: narrowing only works when the check is written inside the if or ?:
Only with an explicit isText: boolean annotation

questions.q: Why does setTimeout(() => email.toLowerCase()) fail with 'email' is possibly 'undefined' after if (email === undefined) return;, when the function later does email = undefined?
questions.explain: Narrowing describes a point in the code. A callback runs at another point. When the variable is not reassigned after the callback is created, TypeScript keeps the narrowing; here it is, so the compiler correctly refuses.
options: Because arrow functions never see narrowing
Because the callback runs later, and the variable is assigned again after the callback is created, so it may be undefined by then
Because email should have been declared with var

questions.q: This compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: TypeScript assumes a function call does not undo narrowing on properties, so order.discount is still treated as a number. At runtime it was deleted, and calling .valueOf() on undefined throws. Read the property into a const before calling other functions.

questions.q: What is the simplest habit that protects you from stale property narrowing like order.discount above?
questions.explain: A const cannot change behind your back, so narrowing on it is always true. ! would only hide the problem.
options: Copy the property into a const, check the const, and use it

questions.q: What does the return type payment is CardPayment tell TypeScript?
questions.explain: A type predicate narrows in both directions: to the type on true, and to the rest of the union on false. TypeScript does not verify the body; it trusts it.
options: That the function converts a payment into a CardPayment
That when the function returns true, the argument is a CardPayment, and when it returns false, it is not
That the function throws unless the argument is a CardPayment
That TypeScript should check the function body against CardPayment

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: filter keeps the original order. Because isConfirmed is a type guard, the filtered array is typed as confirmed bookings only, so b.seat compiles.

questions.q: With TypeScript 5.5 or later, what is the type of present in const present = [1, undefined, 3].filter((x) => x !== undefined);?
questions.explain: TypeScript 5.5 infers x is number for a simple arrow function whose body is a check it can read both ways, so filter uses its type-guard overload.

questions.q: This compiles. What does it print?
questions.explain: The predicate claims "false means not a number", but 900 is a number that returned false. TypeScript believes the predicate, so in that path it types amount as string; only the runtime typeof reveals the truth. Predicates must mean exactly "is this type".
options: review | text 900 | a number slipped through

questions.q: What is the difference between a type guard (value is T) and an assertion function (asserts value is T)?
questions.explain: Both are ordinary runtime functions. Use a guard when you want to choose what to do with bad values, and an assertion function when bad values should stop the work.
options: There is none; they are two spellings of the same thing
A guard returns a boolean and narrows inside the if you write; an assertion function throws on failure and narrows every line after the call
A guard runs at compile time and an assertion function at runtime
An assertion function converts the value; a guard only checks it

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: asserts condition narrows by the expression you pass: after the first call, amount is a number, so amount > 0 compiles. Each failed assertion throws its own message.
options:
2500
amount is required
amount must be positive

2500
amount must be positive
amount must be positive

questions.q: const assertPositive = (n: number): asserts n => { … } compiles, but calling assertPositive(5) gives error TS2775. Why?
questions.explain: Control-flow analysis needs to know from the declaration alone that a call can narrow. Use a function declaration, or annotate the const with a function type that includes asserts.
options: Assertion functions must be called through a name with an explicitly written type; this const has only an inferred type
asserts n needs n to be a boolean

questions.q: A form sends "abc" as an amount. Number("abc") gives NaN. Which check catches it?
questions.explain: NaN has type number, and typeof NaN is "number", so no type check can tell. Number.isFinite is false for NaN and the infinities.

questions.q: In a switch (payment.kind) that handles every kind, what does default: { const unhandled: never = payment; … } give you?
questions.explain: When every kind is handled, payment is never in the default branch, so the assignment is fine. A new unhandled kind is not assignable to never, and the compiler points straight at the switch.
options: A compile error at that line as soon as a new kind is added without a case
It converts unknown kinds to never at runtime
It is required, otherwise switch does not narrow

questions.q: You wrote isNuban(value: unknown): value is string for ten-digit account numbers. Which test table is most useful?
questions.explain: The compiler trusts a guard's body, so tests are the only check. The values that are almost right, and the ones typeof gets wrong, are where guards break.
options: A valid one, nine and eleven digits, a number instead of a string, a string with a space, null and an array
No tests are needed, because tsc checks the predicate

questions.q: Why is const card = payment as CardPayment; not a substitute for narrowing?
questions.explain: A type assertion compiles to nothing. If payment is a wallet payment, card.last4 is undefined at runtime. The next lesson covers as in detail.
options: Because as performs no check at all; it only changes what the compiler believes
Because as converts the value, which can lose data
Because as is removed only in production builds

questions.q: Finish toKobo(amount: number | string): number. Strings are trimmed and converted with Number. If the result is not finite or is not greater than 0, return -1. Otherwise return the amount in kobo (naira × 100), rounded to a whole number.
questions.explain: typeof picks the format, but the type system cannot see NaN, so Number.isFinite does that part. Rounding keeps kobo whole even when 12.5 * 100 is not exact.

questions.q: Finish stockLine without using truthiness on the quantity: a missing item prints unknown item, 0 prints out of stock, and anything else prints N in stock.
questions.explain: !quantity treats "not in the list" and "none left" the same. Compare with undefined and with 0 explicitly, and each fact gets its own branch.
questions.expected:
12 in stock
out of stock
unknown item

questions.q: Finish receipt with a switch on kind. Cards print card *LAST4: AMOUNT, transfers transfer REFERENCE: AMOUNT, wallets wallet PHONE: AMOUNT.
questions.explain: Inside each case, payment is narrowed to one member, so only that member's properties can be read. Because every kind is handled, no final return is needed.

questions.q: Write a type guard isNuban(value: unknown): value is string that is true only for strings of exactly ten digits. Then print how many of the inputs pass.
questions.explain: Check the type first with typeof, then the format. ^ and $ make the pattern match the whole string, so nine or eleven digits fail.

questions.q: Write an assertion function assertAccountId(value: unknown): asserts value is string that throws a TypeError with the message bad id unless the value is a string matching ACC- followed by five digits.
questions.explain: With the asserts value is string return type, input is a string on the line after the call, so input.toLowerCase() compiles without String(…).

questions.q: Finish explain(error: unknown): an InsufficientFundsError prints top up N (its shortBy), any other Error prints failed: MESSAGE, and anything else prints failed: followed by String(error).
questions.explain: Errors are unknown, so narrow them with instanceof, most specific class first. A thrown string is not an Error, so it needs its own fallback.
questions.expected:
top up 2500
failed: amount too large
failed: timeout

questions.q: Finish effectiveLimit(limit: number | undefined): a missing limit means the default 50000, but 0 must stay 0. Use one operator.
questions.explain: ?? only replaces null and undefined, so a limit of 0 survives. || replaces every falsy value.

questions.q: Finish recipient(to: string | null | undefined): with one check using == null, return none for both null and undefined; otherwise return to trimmed.
questions.explain: to == null is true for null and undefined only, and TypeScript removes both, so to.trim() compiles. Unlike if (!to), it would keep an empty string as a real value.
